### jvmcontract: a regression check runs each version on its own dependency closure and over an interface parameter, for example 285's preservation (verification pending)

change `lustnxwmkxvs` · [log `b2fed0906cef`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/b2fed0906cefc1e3dd894c9f45f39959dccafb37e985c5cf4dcf6f88aa0b5920.jsonl.gz)

Example 285's preservation task (Spring Boot 2.7.17 against 2.7.18, WebMvcTags.method(HttpServletRequest), the known-method-labels-preserved claim) was not executed: the two releases have dependency closures of other bytes, and jvmcontract's equivalence took one class path for both (VF-027's verifier-interface:two-dependency-closures). Behind that refusal a regression check also made no input of an interface type and compared two results of an interface type by Objects.equals, which says nothing about objects of two relocated classes. The regression check is extended so that the frozen claim is decided as stated, each release on its own pinned closure.

What changed in lib/:
- equivalence --before-classpath gives the previous version a dependency closure of its own (relocate::with_closure). Its build is relocated under before/ as always, and with it every class of its closure that the build names, directly or through the closure's classes in turn (a class entry, a descriptor or a generic signature of the constant pool), so both versions run in one program, each on its own libraries. A class only the new closure has is renamed in the previous version's references too, to a class that does not exist, so the previous version never runs on the new version's. Nothing is shared between two closures, JDK classes apart. Without the option both versions run on --classpath, as before.
- A parameter of an interface type is given an implementation in a regression check as in a property check (src/given.rs): one generated class per version, answering the accessors either version may call, the two objects made from the same values. A given implementation's fields are final, so nothing of it is compared after the calls.
- A result of an interface type that the previous version has its own copy of is compared through the interface's accessors, a String by content, two nulls agreeing; the statement says so. An interface with an abstract method that is no accessor, or with none, is refused by name (given::unread).
- --unchanged-unless reads a given object as Java does, on the new version's (request != null && !request.getMethod().equals("GET")). An input on which the expression throws is not among those the change is meant for, so the versions are compared on it. Such an expression beside an object made by its constructor is refused by name.
- JBMC is given neither a given implementation nor a closure of the previous version's own: --engine jbmc and --confirm are refused by name, as are --before-target, --before-arguments, --results-agree-when and a correspondence over an interface parameter.

examples/tools/targets/runtime.py passes the previous revision's dependencies as --before-classpath when the pair's closures differ, where it refused the pair before; a pair with one closure of the same bytes is run as before.

Unit tests of the closure relocation, of the abstract methods accessors leave unread, and of the previous descriptor; the JBMC refusals in conformance.rs's pending test; a unit test of the route's command line for one closure, two and none. The default run passed, 34 of 34, before a last addition to the statement's words (the thrown declared change, only where a given implementation is among the inputs), after which the unit tests and the two interface test files were run again.

### jvmcontract: claims javac compiles, String and String[] inputs, String, stream and regex models, induction and lemmas, for example 286's decision claim (verification pending)

change `zrzuurtknzpv` · [log `f720acba22b4`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/f720acba22b42aec0b3ce3431e36902d54676d6e2ea5e53f49b4e5bebed98440.jsonl.gz)

Example 286 (CVE-2022-22968, Spring Framework 5.3.18 to 5.3.19) states its decision claim in Java over the adapter entry allowed(String[] allowedPatterns, String[] disallowedPatterns, String field): a field some disallowed pattern matches ignoring ASCII case is denied, the match written with streams, lambdas and java.util.regex. Until now jvmcontract refused it at the String[] parameters, at the expressions, and at every String, StringBuilder, stream and regex call on the way. With this change the unchanged claim is proved on 5.3.19 and refuted on 5.3.18 and on the constructed mutant at small bounds inline (3 code units and 3 elements: 8 s, 7 s and 6 s in an unoptimized build), each witness run in the harness on a JVM; the frozen bound of 8 is queued.

What a property check gained. A String parameter is a String of its own of at most --max-array-length code units, and a String[] an array of such Strings or nulls. An assumption or assertion the tool's own expression compiler does not take is compiled by javac into a class beside the harness and run as bytecode, as the target is; a witness of such a claim is run in the harness on a JVM, so a refutation rests on Java's own libraries and not on a model. prove --decreases EXPR proves a method that calls itself by induction on a measure: a recursive call on arguments within the assumption and the bound whose measure is smaller is taken to satisfy the property, and any other recursive call ends the check with no verdict. prove --lemmas FILE proves each lemma first and then lets its statement stand in for the calls of its method where the arguments are within the bound it was proved at, the method running as written elsewhere; a method that writes a field or compares its arguments by identity is refused as a lemma's subject.

What the own checker gained. String.substring, indexOf, endsWith, toLowerCase on ASCII (under the stated assumption that the default locale is not Turkish, Azeri or Lithuanian), split at one character and chars; StringBuilder's constructors, length, indexOf, substring, delete and toString; lambdas, method references and four stream model classes run as the loops they stand for; Pattern.quote, String.join, Pattern.compile, matcher and matches as far as a claim states a glob with them, a pattern held as its pieces so that a case-insensitive match and an exact match of lower-cased Strings are one formula; class literals, Class.forName and the class path's loader under a stated assumption, for spring-jcl's logging probes. Each new String method has an evidence record in values::OPERATIONS (String model 3) whose 85 boundary cases give one outcome on the JVM, in the interpreter and in the checker; the interpreter's substring and toLowerCase now return the JDK's objects (the String itself, the literal empty String). What a model takes for granted about the JVM is listed among a statement's assumptions.

Paths. Once more than 1024 paths have been explored (Options::merge_heaps_after), paths whose heaps are not of one shape are merged into the union of their heaps, each first rid of dead locals and unreachable objects; a loop's exit is then a join, and waiting paths are resumed in the order of the loops they are in. Below that count the engine merges as before. The count is a measured compromise: merging heaps from the first path took the values sweep's list totals from 0.07 s to over a minute at 6 lines, since the two sums are then no longer one formula by gate hashing, and waiting for 1024 paths costs example 286's decision 1.7 times its time at 5 code units against 512. An array of computed size is taken within one more than the bound (a table over a bounded String's positions).

Two leaks found by the default run and closed. The new StringBuilder, Class and ArrayList models had been added to gaps::exact_jdk_call, which JBMC's gap listing and the contract reader also ask: JBMC's stubs for those calls would have counted as exact, and a contract for StringBuilder.&lt;init>() was refused. They are now gaps::modelled_jdk_call, the own checker's alone, and a contract given for a modelled call is applied in place of the model, so the three contract tests of lib/tests/integration.rs pass unchanged. And a call the checker has no model of on a builder it holds the content of (append, reverse) now drops that content: a later modelled call on the builder is refused by name instead of answering from stale content.

examples/286-.../proofs/prove.py TASK runs vulnerable-security, fixed-security or mutant-security from target.json and the frozen claim file, on the revision's pinned JARs (each checked against its SHA-256) with the adapter compiled against them, and builds the mutant as sources.lock.json says. proofs/simple-match.contract is the lemma: PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatch on ASCII Strings is the claim's own regular expression, by induction on the pattern's length. These are proofs beside the example route, which runs the verifier on the original artifact alone and still stops at DataBinder's receiver (VF-027); the example's records are not changed in this commit and follow with the results.

### CLAUDE.md: a probe of a prover or model checker may run inline up to 5 minutes and 4 GB, under a cap

change `upkxonlzouws` · [log `9f9d2f78e7ad`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/9f9d2f78e7ad4959dacc5eee283e86dcf2cd141a71f1afa944b6448db2b3261f.jsonl.gz)

At the user's request: the 1 GB line between inline runs and verification jobs had agents tuning a checker's memory to fit a quick probe before knowing whether the real proof works (prove-examples, example 287), and real-world claims often need more than 1 GB just to show where a checker stops. A single probe on one claim may now run inline, one at a time, for up to 5 minutes and 4 GB, inside systemd-run --scope with MemoryMax=4G and a timeout, so it cannot take more. A run that needs more is still a job, and the default test run and the tool tier keep their 1 GB. CLAUDE.md and verification/README.md say the same.

The tool's own checker stopped at the claim's regular expression, at the text-to-bytes calls and at bcrypt's loops, which go round 18, 512, 2^cost and 64 times against --unwind 16. It now runs the claims as they are written. A loop that goes round more often than the bound is covered by an invariant the checker finds and proves by induction (lib/src/bmc/loops.rs: what one iteration writes is set to any value, candidate facts about each written number are dropped until the rest is kept by an iteration, and the loop is shown to end by a counter or said not to be); a verdict names the loops so covered, a violation past one is believed only when its witness, the least violating input, reproduces on a JVM, and otherwise the answer is no verdict with the loop named. Also new: String.matches and Pattern.compile of a constant regular expression with classes, groups, alternatives and counts (lib/src/bmc/regex.rs); String.getBytes(UTF_8), MessageDigest.isEqual, Arrays.copyOf, Integer.parseInt and StringBuilder's charAt and appends (lib/src/bmc/bytes.rs, strings.rs); Object.getClass of an object the run made, String.toString, an initializer that keeps method references, and a throws clause whose condition javac compiles. The solver side defers clauses until a call depends on them, checks lazy divisions only in the cone a question reads, and shares a path's models by pages. The search for the least witness takes at most half the time the run has left, so a violation found late is not lost to it.

The String model is model 4, the reference calls model 2: getBytes, matches and toString have evidence records sampled on the JVM and in the checker (lib/tests/values.rs), the gap scan counts Pattern.compile of a constant in the checker's syntax as reproduced, and the interpreter's String.toString returns the String itself. Tests that relied on a class regex, toString or a builder append being a gap now use forms that still are (a reluctant or possessive quantifier, trim, append(CharSequence), append(long)); the calibration fixture's RegexGate uses a possessive quantifier and its records were remade. New tests: lib/tests/loops.rs (four, on a small fixture with the same loop shapes), three in lib/tests/claims.rs (each model against a definition written out in Java and sampled on a JVM), three unit tests in bits.rs. ### 4. 2026-11-15 17:38 UTC

> I like chaining the sessions because future sessions learn implicitly from previous sessions -- this is by design. I think auto compaction is probably the way to go. If we hit auto compact without a commit, then it requires user input. In theory, this should only happen in earlier cycles as later cycles benefit from the foundation that was previously built. I don't like adding any extraneous information to moonshot input because it defeats the purpose of experimenting. I am thinking 600k is a reasonable limit. Can this be updated while the current loop is running so as not to disrupt it?

**Reply:**

No, the running loop can't pick up the change. Its bash parsed the whole cycle loop when it started, so nothing written to the script now reaches it. But you can apply the change at a cycle boundary without losing anything. I've made the change and committed it in the side workspace `moonshot`, where it can't touch the loop's working copy.

## The change (`uzporttn`)
- **600k limit:** every moonshot turn passes `--autocompact 600k`. Briefs are left alone because they have their own stopping rules. `FEATURE_LOOP_AUTOCOMPACT` overrides the value; claude accepts 100k to 1M.
- **Compaction with no commit stops the loop:**
  - The loop watches the instruction turn for an automatic compaction. If no commit has landed since the cycle began, or since the previous compaction, it ends the turn right there, which is between model calls, and stops claude's child processes too.
  - It then writes "Stopped …: cycle N (item X) compacted with no commit at T tokens; session … needs attention" to the run record and exits.
- **Unchanged:** sessions stay chained across cycles, and the moonshot prompt gets nothing added. Manual `/compact` turns and the end-of-run summary turn aren't watched.
- **Stats:** `loop_stats.py` counts this as a new stop reason, "compacted, no commit".

**How I tested it:** I put a stand-in `claude` on PATH that emits a compaction event.
- Auto compaction with no commit: the turn ended immediately, no child process was left behind, and the stop reason was written.

> Make a note for conductor brief -- we will likely want a moonshot conductor, that makes some qualitative judgment on compact (i.e., whether it's compacting because the work is really hard but still making good progress, or whether stuck and requiring human input) and acts on it. This judgment should come from outside of the primary moonshoot loop so as not to distract it and seems like a good fit
>
> *… (shortened; the log has the full text)*

**Reply:**

I've added the moonshot conductor to the conductor brief as **Design 7** and **plan step 7**, committed as `ulzlppqm` in the `stream-conductor` workspace with a plain `jj commit`. The current loop keeps running untouched.

**What the brief now says:**
- **The problem:** a moonshot has no acceptance criteria. Sessions stay chained by design, the one-line input gets nothing added, and leaving an item unfinished is fine if the work was productive, since a later pass can return to it.
- **The judgment:** at each automatic compaction, a separate session outside the moonshot loop decides whether the work is hard but still going well, or stuck and needing a person. It reads the transcript, the commits and diff, test runs, jobs, and whether the same failure keeps coming back. Keeping it outside means the moonshot isn't distracted, which fits the conductor's purpose.
- **The actions:** by default it lets the turn go on. If the session is stuck, it stops the loop and queues a decision for you saying why. The brief leaves other actions for the implementer to propose, such as ending the item at its last good commit. Every judgment goes into the decision record with its reasoning.
- **The fallback:** the mechanical stop in `uzporttn` (600k limit, stop on a compaction with no commit) applies when the conductor isn't running or can't decide. The brief notes that `show_progress` already sees the compaction event and holds claude's process id, so that's where the hand-off goes.

> The moonshot workspace may have some changes designed to address this, and is likely simpler / more effective to apply than conductor. Can you confirm or deny this?

**Reply:**

It's partly true. The moonshot workspace holds one change, `uzporttn`: the 600k compaction limit plus the rule that stops the loop when an automatic compaction comes with no commit. It's simpler than the conductor, but it would have handled this cycle worse.

**What it would have done in cycle 2:**
- **More room first.** Compaction would have come at about 600k tokens instead of 469k. The extra ~130k might have been enough for the agent to reach a commit, and then nothing would have stopped.

### 26. 2026-11-16 03:29 UTC

> Should we relax the 1GB memory limit? This can easily go to 4GB (or higher), especially as real world changes can be much more complex

**Reply:**

Yes, I'd relax it, but for one-off probes only, and with a hard cap. Some background first.

**Where the 1 GB comes from:** it isn't a limit in the checker. It's the line in `CLAUDE.md:20` (repeated in `verification/README.md:57`) between what an agent may run during its turn and what it must queue as a verification job. The checker itself can already use much more as a job. The trouble is that the agent's quick probes must stay under 1 GB, so it ends up tuning memory to pass that line before it knows whether the real proof works. That's what happened at 03:12–03:16.

To be fair, the two fixes it made there would matter at any limit: 32k fresh variables for every store into an unknown array, and dense per-path models. Real changes would hit both. But the next round of that kind of tuning would mostly be work to satisfy the rule.

**What I'd change:**
1. **Agent probes:** a single inline run of the checker may use up to **4 GB and a few minutes**, inside a `systemd-run` scope with `MemoryMax=4G`. The agent already runs its probes in such scopes, so the cap is easy to enforce. During 286 one of them was killed for running out of memory at its 2 GiB cap, and the loop carried on unharmed.
2. **Tool-tier tests stay at 1 GB.** The default run starts many tests at once, so 4 GB each would overrun the loop's memory. Real-world-sized proofs stay as jobs, as now.
3. **Jobs** need no change. They already declare their memory, and the runner has 80G while one loop runs.

The new probe limit is in place and the loop is unaffected. It takes effect from cycle 4: the running cycle 3 process loaded `CLAUDE.md` when it started and won't reload it.

**The rule** (commit `upkxonlz`, in `CLAUDE.md` with the same text in `verification/README.md`):
- A single run of a prover or model checker on one claim may now run inline, one at a time, for up to **5 minutes and 4 GB**.
- It has to run under a cap it can't exceed: `systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=4G -p MemorySwapMax=0 timeout 300 COMMAND`. The agent already ran its probes this way, with a 2G cap.
- The rule tells agents not to tune memory or time just to fit under the cap. A run that needs more is still a job.
- The default test run and the tool tier keep their 1 GB.

- **Commit:** made in the `moonshot` workspace as a plain `jj commit`, so the loop's working copy was never touched. The `moonshot` workspace is back on uzporttn.
